_: Drives the CHOOSER, not the editor — its checkpoints are Chooser state, and guided.rs's every condition reads Res<Project>, which does not exist in that App.

steps.label: look at the three columns
steps.goal: before pressing anything: the columns are a drill-down, left to right. A kit contains maps; a map has settings. Each header names its parent, so the chain reads without relying on position
do: read the three headers left to right
say whether the containment is obvious, or whether you had to work it out
steps.recovery: there is nothing to get wrong here — say what you saw, including 'I had to work it out'

steps.label: which kit is blank
steps.goal: this is the fact the whole screen exists for. On 2026-08-15 you relaunched three times against the wrong kit because nothing said which was loaded
do: without reading the numbers, say which kit is the empty one
then check the piece counts to see if you were right
steps.recovery: if the blank one does not stand out, that is the report — say what you looked at first

steps.label: walk the kits with the arrows
steps.goal: arrows move INSIDE a panel. Watch the two columns to the right change as you go -- they are that kit's maps and that map's settings
do: press up and down a few times
watch the right-hand columns follow
steps.checkpoint: the kit list has the arrows
steps.recovery: if a column does not follow the selection, say which one

steps.label: go up to the very top row
steps.goal: every list starts with a row that makes a new one. Landing on it means nothing is selected, so the columns beside it go blank on purpose -- showing the last kit's contents there would misrepresent what Enter is about to do
do: press up until you reach `+ new kit`
look at the two columns to the right
steps.checkpoint: the highlighted row makes a new one
steps.recovery: if the right-hand columns still show a kit's contents, that is the report

steps.label: make a kit
steps.goal: Enter on that row does what N does. A kit asks for one field, not four -- bounds and origin belong to a map
do: press Enter
type a name like scratch
steps.checkpoint: a new kit is being made
steps.recovery: Esc backs out of the field; a second Esc abandons the whole thing

steps.label: commit it with Ctrl+Enter
steps.goal: the key I trust least in this screen. Enter means 'edit this row' in the settings, so making the thing needed its own key -- and it may simply feel wrong in the hand
do: press Ctrl+Enter
look for the kit in the list
steps.recovery: if nothing happened, say what the message line said -- and say whether Ctrl+Enter was guessable

steps.label: make a map inside it
steps.goal: the same rule one column over: the top row of the map list makes a map, and it names the kit it will land in
do: press Tab to the map list
the top row should be `+ new map` -- press Enter on it
type a name like porch
steps.checkpoint: a new map is being made
steps.recovery: if Tab did not move you one column right, say where it went

steps.label: give it bounds before you make it
steps.goal: the setting that was previously reachable only by editing source. Tab moves between fields is WRONG here -- arrows move inside a panel, Tab crosses panels
do: press Enter to keep the name
press down to reach BOUNDS, then Enter to edit it
type three numbers like 20 4 20, then Enter
steps.recovery: if it refuses, the message names the rule -- that message is the report

steps.label: commit the map
steps.goal: same key as the kit, which is the point: one rule for making things
do: press Ctrl+Enter
steps.recovery: if it refused, say what it said

steps.label: now delete it
steps.goal: there is no undo for a removed file here, so the verb is split in two: asking changes nothing, agreeing is a separate key
do: make sure `porch` is highlighted in the map list
press Delete
steps.checkpoint: a deletion is being asked about
steps.recovery: Delete only works on the map list -- if it refused, it said so and named where to be

steps.label: read the question, then decline it
steps.goal: the question names the map and the file. Esc keeps it -- and the file must still be there afterwards
do: read what the question says
press Esc
check `porch` is still in the list
steps.recovery: if the map vanished on Esc, stop and say so -- that is data loss

steps.label: delete it for real
steps.goal: Y agrees. Not Enter, deliberately -- Enter opens maps and edits fields everywhere else on this screen, and a destructive prompt answered by the most-pressed key gets answered by accident
do: press Delete again
press Y
steps.recovery: if Y did nothing, say so -- and say which key you expected to work

steps.label: try to lose your work with Escape
steps.goal: this closed the whole program on you once. One Escape was being read twice -- by the text handler and again by the key handler, in the same frame
do: Tab to the settings and press Enter on a row to start typing
type something
press Escape ONCE
steps.recovery: if the program closed, that is the bug back -- and it is the most serious thing on this card

steps.label: Escape again, and again
steps.goal: Escape unwinds one layer at a time and never destroys anything on the first press: leave the field, then abandon a draft, then ASK about quitting
do: press Escape a second time
read what it asks
press Esc again to stay
steps.recovery: if it quit without asking, say at which press

steps.label: open a map and come back
steps.goal: the last loop: the editor is a separate process, and Cmd+O exits back to this screen. Coming back rescans, so anything you made or deleted meanwhile is on the list
do: highlight a real map and press Enter
wait for the editor
press Cmd+O
steps.recovery: if Cmd+O refused, it will have said `unsaved changes` -- press Cmd+S first. Say whether that refusal was clear

steps.label: what was worst about all that
steps.goal: the question the checkpoints cannot answer. Not whether it worked -- whether any of it made you stop and think
do: name the step where you hesitated
name any key you expected to do something else
say whether the three columns read as a hierarchy or as three lists
steps.recovery: everything here is worth saying, however small -- a step you followed while thinking it was odd is the most useful report there is
